newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish coalition row brings talk of early polls.
newsitem.headline: Polish coalition row brings talk of early polls.

text.p: Poland's Peasant party (PSL) accused its larger ex-communist partner on Thursday of sacking a Peasant party minister in a bid to sabotage their two-party ruling coalition and force early parliamentary elections.
"After such a humiliation, we might quit the government," a Peasant leader, Aleksander Bentkowski, said in response to the sudden firing of Foreign Trade Minister Jacek Buchacz.
"If the coalition breaks up, we will have early elections in spring. This is very likely," he told Gazeta Wyborcza daily.
The government said on Wednesday Buchacz had been dismissed by the president, on a motion from Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz of the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).

It said official investigations had revealed "involvement of the treasury in ventures concerning export guarantees, in which state and private property is connected in a way that lacks sufficient clarity".
PSL chiefs said their party would meet on Friday to decide whether to hold further talks with the ex-communist SLD.
Senior Peasant deputy Janusz Piechocinski told Reuters the sacking, on which his party had not been consulted, might be aimed at provoking his party to quit the coalition.
The SLD could form a minority government, backed by its former chief President Aleksander Kwasniewski, and call polls in April which are otherwise not due until September next year.
Piechocinski said he was suggesting a meeting of both parliamentary parties on Tuesday to thrash out the issue.
Jozef Oleksy, head of the SLD's core party, told Reuters the PSL allegations were unfounded and he did not expect the coalition to collapse, but everything was up to the Peasants.
"At the moment I do not rule out any scenario," he said.
President Kwasniewski also said he did not think the row would prompt early polls as not enough deputies were in favour.
"I believe Premier Cimoszewicz, a sensible man, and the leadership of the PSL and SLD who are also responsible people, will find a solution," PAP news agency quoted him as saying.
The exact allegations against Buchacz, raised in probes by official oversight bodies, were not revealed.
Earlier this year the government rejected plans by Buchacz to set up a new export guarantee system and told him to wait until proper rules had been laid down.
Buchacz has incurred criticism for forming treasury-controlled companies to which he allocated shares kept by the state after privatisation of other firms.
The new companies aim to provide export guarantees or invest in other firms, public and state-owned.
The PSL's Piechocinski conceded that Buchacz might have some explaining to do over certain of his decisions.
But he said the minister's goal had been to boost exports and stop Poland's official foreign trade deficit from swelling to $10 billion by end-1996, from $1.8 billion last year.

The two parties, rooted in the old communist system, have stayed in coalition through two cabinet reshuffles and several grave rows since 1993 polls in which they defeated parties which grew out of the pre-1989 anti-communist Solidarity movement.
But their policy differences have grown and the two have recently been quarrelling over the distribution of cabinet posts during a reorganisation of ministries due this year.
The SLD, whose clear lead in opinion polls has been slipping, argued earlier this year for spring 1997 elections, while the less-popular Peasants argued for a September vote.

Both parties flirt with the idea of forming alternative alliances with opposition groups, although parties descended from the pre-1989 anti-communist movement have so far shunned formal cooperation with the ex-communist SLD.
